title: focus
summary: Lesson 11 reviews the main ideas of calculus and shows how limits, derivatives, and integrals work together to solve real‑world problems. Students will practice linking these tools across physics, biology, and economics contexts.
objectives: Identify how limits, derivatives, and integrals are connected
Apply each calculus tool to a simple physics, biology, or economics scenario
Explain why choosing the right tool matters for a given problem
Solve a multi‑step problem that uses a limit, a derivative, and an integral
Reflect on the solution process to build confidence in using calculus
prerequisites: Students should already know basic limits, derivative rules, and antiderivative techniques from earlier lessons.
why: Calculus is the language of change. Engineers use limits to predict system behavior, biologists model population growth with derivatives, and economists evaluate profit trends with integrals. Understanding how these tools fit together lets you choose the right method for any situation.

Real‑world problems rarely stay within one calculus topic. By mastering the connections, you can tackle complex tasks—like finding the speed of a car, the rate of drug absorption, or the total cost of production—more efficiently and with greater confidence.

sections.heading: 1. Review of Core Concepts
sections.body:
Recall that a **limit** tells us what value a function $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to as the input $x$ approaches a particular point $a$.  
We write this as  

$$\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L,$$  

meaning “as $x$ gets nearer and nearer to $a$, the outputs $f(x)$ get nearer and nearer to $L$.”  
Think of a car approaching a stop sign: the car’s speed may never actually become zero until it stops, but we can describe the speed it is *approaching* as it gets closer to the sign. The limit captures that “approaching” idea without requiring the function to actually reach the value at $a$.

> **Definition:** A limit $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L$ exists if we can make $f(x)$ as close as we wish to $L$ by choosing $x$ sufficiently close (but not equal) to $a$.

The **derivative** measures how fast a function changes at a single point. Formally, it is the limit of the average rate of change over a shrinking interval:

$$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.$$

Here $h$ is a tiny step away from $a$, and the fraction $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ is the slope of the secant line joining $(a,f(a))$ and $(a+h,f(a+h))$. As $h$ shrinks, the secant line tilts toward the **tangent line**, the straight line that just touches the curve at $(a,f(a))$ without crossing it. The slope of this tangent line is the derivative $f'(a)$.

> **In daily life:** If $f(t)$ gives the distance a runner has traveled after $t$ minutes, then $f'(t)$ is the runner’s instantaneous speed at that exact minute—how fast the distance is changing right then.

An **antiderivative** (also called an indefinite integral) works in the opposite direction. It is a function $F(x)$ whose derivative returns the original function $f(x)$:

$$F'(x)=f(x).$$

Because adding a constant $C$ does not change the derivative, every antiderivative comes in a family $F(x)+C$. Geometrically, $F(x)$ can be thought of as the “area under the curve” of $f$ measured from a fixed starting point, though that interpretation becomes precise when we move to definite integrals later.

> **Note:** The antiderivative is not a single function but a whole set of functions that differ only by a constant.

Why are these ideas useful together? The limit gives us a rigorous way to talk about “instantaneous” behavior, which the derivative captures as a single number—the slope of the tangent. The antiderivative then tells us how to reconstruct the original function from its slopes. This three‑part relationship—limit → derivative → antiderivative—forms the backbone of calculus.

Consider a simple parabola $f(x)=x^{2}$. Its limit as $x$ approaches $3$ is $\lim_{x\to3}x^{2}=9$. Using the definition of the derivative,

$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(x+h)^{2}-x^{2}}{h}
       =\lim_{h\to0}\frac{2xh+h^{2}}{h}
       =\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h)=2x,$$

so at $x=3$ the slope of the tangent line is $f'(3)=6$. An antiderivative of $f$ is $F(x)=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C$, because differentiating $F$ gives back $x^{2}$.

> **Remember:** A limit describes a value we get *close to*; a derivative is the *instantaneous rate of change* found by a limit; an antiderivative is a function whose *derivative brings us back* to the original.

Keeping these geometric pictures in mind—approaching a point, a tangent line touching a curve, and a curve built up from tiny sloping pieces—will help you see how limits, derivatives, and antiderivatives fit together as tools for describing change.

sections.heading: 2. The Relationship Between Limits and Derivatives
sections.body:
When we talk about a **derivative**, we are really asking one question: *How fast is something changing at this exact instant?*  
To answer that, we look at the change over a very short time interval, then let that interval become *as small as possible*. The tool that lets us do this is the **limit**.

> **Definition:** The derivative of a function $f$ at a point $x=a$ is the limit of the difference quotient  
> $$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.$$

The expression inside the limit, $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$, is called the **difference quotient**. It measures the average rate of change of $f$ over the interval from $a$ to $a+h$. Think of $h$ as a tiny step forward on the $x$‑axis. The numerator $f(a+h)-f(a)$ tells us how much the function’s value rises (or falls) during that step, and dividing by $h$ spreads that change out over the length of the step, giving an average slope.

Why do we let $h$ go to zero? Imagine you are driving and you want to know your speed at a particular instant, not just the average speed over a mile. If you look at your odometer after a long stretch, you get an average speed. To get the instantaneous speed, you would need to look at the distance covered in an *infinitesimally* short time. The limit does exactly that: it shrinks the interval until the average slope becomes the true slope at the single point.

### Step‑by‑step example

Let’s find the derivative of the simple function $f(x)=x^{2}$ at the point $x=3$.

1. **Write the difference quotient.**  
   $$\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} = \frac{(3+h)^{2}-3^{2}}{h}.$$

2. **Expand the numerator.**  
   $(3+h)^{2}=9+6h+h^{2}$, so  
   $$\frac{9+6h+h^{2}-9}{h}= \frac{6h+h^{2}}{h}.$$

3. **Factor out $h$ from the numerator.**  
   $$\frac{h(6+h)}{h}.$$

4. **Cancel the common factor $h$ (provided $h\neq0$).**  
   $$6+h.$$

5. **Take the limit as $h\to0$.**  
   $$\lim_{h\to0}(6+h)=6.$$

Thus $f'(3)=6$. In words, the slope of the parabola $y=x^{2}$ at $x=3$ is $6$; the function is increasing six units in $y$ for each one unit you move to the right in $x$ at that exact spot.

> **In daily life:** If you picture a hill shaped like $y=x^{2}$, the derivative at a point tells you how steep the hill feels right under your feet. Standing at $x=3$, the hill feels as steep as a slope of $6$ (rise $6$ meters for every meter you walk forward).

> **Note:** The limit only exists if the left‑hand and right‑hand approaches give the same number. If they differ, the function has no derivative there (a corner or cusp).

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to cancel the $h$ before taking the limit. If you try to plug $h=0$ directly into $\frac{6h+h^{2}}{h}$ you get $\frac{0}{0}$, an undefined expression. Cancelling first simplifies the fraction so the limit can be evaluated.

### Why this matters

Knowing that a derivative is a limit of a difference quotient connects two core ideas of calculus: **limits** (the language of approaching) and **rates of change** (the language of derivatives). This bridge lets us move from geometric notions of slope to algebraic formulas we can compute, and later to the reverse process—integrals—where we add up infinitely many tiny pieces.

> **Remember:** The derivative $f'(a)$ is *the* limit of the average slope as the interval shrinks to zero. It gives the exact instantaneous rate of change at $x=a$.

sections.heading: 3. From Derivatives to Integrals
sections.body:
When we first met derivatives, we thought of them as “instantaneous rates of change.”  
If $f(t)$ tells us the position of a car at time $t$, then $f'(t)$ tells us the car’s speed at that exact moment.  

Now imagine we know the speed function $v(t)=f'(t)$ and we want to recover the original position $f(t)$.  
The **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC)** tells us exactly how to do that: it says that integration, the process of adding up tiny pieces, is the inverse operation of differentiation.

> **Definition:** *Fundamental Theorem of Calculus* –  
> If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $F$ is any function whose derivative is $f$ (that is, $F'(x)=f(x)$), then  
> $$\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a).$$  

In words, the total accumulated change of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ equals the difference between the values of an antiderivative $F$ at the endpoints.  

Why does this work? Think of the interval $[a,b]$ as a road. The derivative $f(x)$ tells us the slope of the road at each point – how steep it is. If we slice the road into many tiny pieces of length $\Delta x$, the change in height over each piece is approximately $f(x_i)\,\Delta x$. Adding all those little changes gives an estimate of the total height gain. When we let the pieces become infinitely small, the sum becomes the integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, and the exact total change is captured by $F(b)-F(a)$.  

> **In daily life:** Imagine filling a bathtub. The water flow rate $r(t)$ (liters per minute) is like a derivative. The amount of water that has entered after $t$ minutes is the integral $\int_0^{t} r(s)\,ds$. The FTC tells us that if we know a function $R(t)$ whose rate of change is $r(t)$, then the water volume at time $t$ is simply $R(t)-R(0)$.  

The theorem has two parts. The first part guarantees that the integral of a continuous function produces an antiderivative. The second part, the formula shown above, lets us evaluate a definite integral by finding any antiderivative $F$. This is why we often write  

$$\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \bigl[\,F(x)\,\bigr]_{a}^{b} = F(b)-F(a).$$  

Here the brackets $[\,\,]_{a}^{b}$ remind us to plug in the upper limit $b$ and subtract the value at the lower limit $a$.

> **Note:** The function $F$ does not have to be the *only* antiderivative; any one works because any two antiderivatives differ by a constant, and that constant cancels when we compute $F(b)-F(a)$.  

Understanding the FTC gives us a powerful bridge:  

* From a **rate** (derivative) we can find the **total amount** (integral).  
* From a **total amount** we can recover the **average rate** by dividing by the interval length:  
  $$\text{average rate} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx.$$  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to add the “$+C$” when finding an antiderivative for an *indefinite* integral, and then using that incomplete $F$ in the FTC formula. The constant cancels in a definite integral, but you must still write it when solving for $F$ first.  

Because the FTC links differentiation and integration, we can choose the tool that best matches the problem. If a problem gives us a rate and asks for total change, we integrate. If it gives us a total change and asks for the rate at a point, we differentiate.  

> **Remember:** The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus tells us that *adding up tiny changes* (integration) exactly reverses *measuring an instant’s change* (differentiation). This symmetry is the heart of calculus and will appear again whenever we move between motion, growth, area, or any situation where rates and totals interact.

sections.heading: 4. Choosing the Right Tool
sections.body:
When you face a real‑world problem, the first question is **what you want to find out**.  
Is it how something changes at a single instant, or is it the total amount that has accumulated over a period?  
The answer tells you whether a *derivative* or an *integral* (or sometimes both) is the right tool.

> **Definition:** A **derivative** measures the instantaneous rate of change of a quantity.  
> It answers “how fast?” at a particular moment.

> **Definition:** An **integral** adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to give a total.  
> It answers “how much in total?” over an interval.

Below are three brief scenarios. For each we identify the question, choose the appropriate calculus concept, and see why it fits.

---

### 1. Physics – Speed of a falling ball  

A ball is dropped from a height. A sensor records its position $s(t)$ (in meters) at time $t$ (in seconds).  
**Question:** What is the ball’s speed exactly 2 seconds after release?

Speed is the rate at which position changes, so we need the derivative of $s(t)$:

$$v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$$  

Evaluating $v(2)$ gives the instantaneous speed at $t=2\,$s.  
If the position function were $s(t)=5t^{2}$, then

$$v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(5t^{2})=10t,$$

and $v(2)=20\,$m/s.  

> **In daily life:** Think of a car’s speedometer. It shows the derivative of the car’s distance‑travelled curve at that exact moment.

---

### 2. Biology – Total nutrient absorbed  

A plant absorbs nutrients from soil at a rate that depends on time: $r(t)$ grams per hour. The rate varies because sunlight and temperature change throughout the day.  
**Question:** How many grams of nutrient does the plant absorb between 8 am and 2 pm?

Here we need the total amount, so we integrate the rate over the time interval:

$$\text{Total}=\int_{8}^{14} r(t)\,dt.$$  

If the rate were $r(t)=3+0.5t$ (with $t$ measured in hours after 8 am), then

$$\int_{8}^{14} (3+0.5t)\,dt
= \Big[3t+0.25t^{2}\Big]_{8}^{14}
= (42+49)-(24+16)=51\text{ grams}.$$

> **Note:** Integration is like adding up the area under the curve of $r(t)$. Each tiny rectangle represents a small amount of nutrient absorbed in a short time slice.

---

### 3. Economics – Marginal profit and total profit  

A company sells widgets. Its profit function $P(q)$ (in dollars) depends on the number $q$ of widgets produced and sold. The **marginal profit** is the derivative $P'(q)$, the extra profit from selling one more widget.  
**Question A:** What is the extra profit from the 101st widget?  
**Question B:** What is the total profit from producing the first 200 widgets if the profit at zero production is zero?

For Question A we use the derivative:

$$\text{Marginal profit at }q=100 = P'(100).$$  

If $P(q)=5q-0.01q^{2}$, then $P'(q)=5-0.02q$, so $P'(100)=5-2=3$ dollars.

For Question B we need the integral of the marginal profit, which recovers the original profit function (up to a constant). Because $P(0)=0$, the constant is zero:

$$P(200)=\int_{0}^{200} P'(q)\,dq.$$

Carrying out the integral gives the same $P(200)$ as plugging directly into $P(q)$.

> **Remember:** In economics, the derivative gives *marginal* quantities (change per extra unit), while the integral gives the *total* accumulated quantity.

---

### Putting it together  

- Use a **derivative** when the problem asks for a rate, slope, or instantaneous change.  
- Use an **integral** when the problem asks for a total amount, accumulated quantity, or area under a curve.  
- Some problems require both: first differentiate to find a rate, then integrate that rate to recover the total.

By matching the question’s wording to these ideas, you can quickly decide which calculus tool will give the answer you need.

sections.heading: 5. Worked Example: Motion Problem
sections.body:
Imagine a car moving along a straight road. At any moment we might want to know **how fast** it is going (its instantaneous velocity), **how quickly that speed is changing** (its acceleration), and **how far** it has travelled over a time interval.  
All three quantities can be obtained from the same piece of information: the position of the car as a function of time, say  

$$s(t)=5t^{2}+2t+1,$$  

where $s$ is measured in meters and $t$ in seconds.

> **Definition:** *Instantaneous velocity* is the limit of the average velocity over a shrinking time interval. It tells us the exact speed at a single instant.

### Step 1 – Find the instantaneous velocity using a limit  

The average velocity between times $t$ and $t+\Delta t$ is  

$$\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

To get the instantaneous velocity at time $t$, we let the interval $\Delta t$ become *infinitely small* and take a limit:

$$v(t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

Plug the given $s(t)$ into the fraction:

\[
\frac{(5(t+\Delta t)^{2}+2(t+\Delta t)+1)-(5t^{2}+2t+1)}{\Delta t}
\]

Expand the numerator:

\[
\frac{5(t^{2}+2t\Delta t+(\Delta t)^{2})+2t+2\Delta t+1-5t^{2}-2t-1}{\Delta t}
= \frac{10t\Delta t+5(\Delta t)^{2}+2\Delta t}{\Delta t}.
\]

Cancel $\Delta t$:

\[
10t+5\Delta t+2.
\]

Now let $\Delta t\to 0$:

$$v(t)=10t+2.$$

So at any moment $t$, the car’s velocity is $10t+2$ meters per second.

> **In daily life:** This is like checking a speedometer that updates continuously; the limit process is the math behind that smooth reading.

### Step 2 – Differentiate to obtain acceleration  

Acceleration tells us how fast the velocity itself is changing. It is the derivative of $v(t)$ with respect to $t$:

$$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}.$$

Since $v(t)=10t+2$, differentiate term by term:

$$a(t)=10.$$

The acceleration is constant: the car speeds up by $10\ \text{m/s}^2$ at every instant.

> **Note:** Differentiation is the formal name for the limit process we used earlier. Once we have a formula for velocity, taking its derivative gives acceleration directly.

### Step 3 – Integrate to find the distance travelled  

Suppose we want the total distance the car travels from $t=0$ to $t=3$ seconds. Integration is the reverse of differentiation: it adds up infinitely many tiny pieces of motion. The distance $D$ is

$$D=\int_{0}^{3} v(t)\,dt.$$

Insert $v(t)=10t+2$:

$$D=\int_{0}^{3} (10t+2)\,dt.$$

Integrate term by term:

\[
\int (10t)\,dt =5t^{2},\qquad \int 2\,dt =2t.
\]

Thus  

$$D=\Bigl[5t^{2}+2t\Bigr]_{0}^{3}= \bigl(5\cdot 3^{2}+2\cdot 3\bigr)-\bigl(5\cdot0^{2}+2\cdot0\bigr)=45+6=51\ \text{meters}.$$

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to evaluate the antiderivative at both limits. Always subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit.

### Putting it all together  

1. **Limit** → instantaneous velocity $v(t)=10t+2$.  
2. **Derivative** (differentiating $v$) → constant acceleration $a(t)=10$.  
3. **Integral** (adding up $v$ over time) → total distance $51\,$m from $0$ to $3\,$s.

> **Remember:** Limits, derivatives, and integrals are three faces of the same idea—how quantities change and accumulate. Mastering each step lets you move smoothly from position → velocity → acceleration, and back from velocity → distance.

sections.heading: 6. Worked Example: Population Growth
sections.body:
Imagine a town where the number of people does not grow forever. At first, when there are few residents, each family can have many children, so the population rises quickly. As the town becomes crowded, there is less space, food, and jobs, so the growth slows down and eventually levels off.  
This idea is captured by the **logistic model**, a simple formula that describes how a population changes over time while respecting a maximum size, called the *carrying capacity*.

> **Definition:** The *carrying capacity* $K$ is the largest population that the environment can sustain indefinitely.

---

### 1. From a limit to the growth rate  

The *instantaneous growth rate* tells us how fast the population is changing at a particular moment. Mathematically, it is the limit of the average change over a very short time interval.

If $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$, the average change from $t$ to $t+\Delta t$ is  

$$\frac{P(t+\Delta t)-P(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

Taking the limit as $\Delta t\to 0$ gives the **derivative**:

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{P(t+\Delta t)-P(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

This derivative is the instantaneous growth rate, measured in people per unit time.

> **Note:** A derivative is just a precise way of saying “how fast something is changing right now”.

---

### 2. Writing the logistic differential equation  

The logistic model assumes two things:

1. When the population is small, it grows proportionally to its current size. This gives a term $rP$, where $r$ is the *intrinsic growth rate* (how fast the population would grow without limits).
2. As the population approaches $K$, the growth slows down. The slowdown is proportional to both the current size $P$ and the fraction of unused capacity $\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$.

Combining these ideas, the *logistic differential equation* is  

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).$$

Here $r>0$ and $K>0$ are constants that depend on the species and environment.

> **In daily life:** Think of a bathtub filling with water. The faucet supplies water at a constant rate, but as the tub fills, the water level rises more slowly because the space left is smaller. The logistic equation works the same way for populations.

---

### 3. Solving the differential equation (finding $P(t)$)

To predict the future population, we need to *integrate* the equation. First, separate the variables $P$ and $t$:

$$\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)}\,dP = r\,dt.$$

The left side can be split using partial fractions:

$$\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)}=\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}.$$

Now integrate both sides:

$$\int\left(\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}\right)dP = \int r\,dt.$$

Carrying out the integrals gives

$$\ln|P| - \ln|K-P| = rt + C,$$

where $C$ is the constant of integration, determined by the initial population $P(0)=P_0$.

Combine the logarithms:

$$\ln\left(\frac{P}{K-P}\right)=rt + C.$$

Exponentiate to remove the log:

$$\frac{P}{K-P}=Ae^{rt},\qquad A=e^{C}.$$

Solve for $P$:

$$P(t)=\frac{K\,Ae^{rt}}{1+Ae^{rt}}.$$

Use the initial condition $P(0)=P_0$ to find $A$:

$$\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}=A,$$

so $A=\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}$. Substituting back,

$$\boxed{\,P(t)=\frac{K}{1+\left(\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}\,}.$$

This formula predicts the population at any future time $t$.

> **Remember:** The logistic curve starts near exponential growth, then bends and approaches the horizontal line $P=K$ as $t\to\infty$.

---

### 4. Using the model: a concrete example  

Suppose a wildlife reserve can support at most $K=10{,}000$ deer. The intrinsic growth rate is $r=0.4$ per year, and the current population is $P_0=1{,}000$ deer.

First compute the factor $\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}= \frac{9{,}000}{1{,}000}=9$.

The population after $t$ years is

$$P(t)=\frac{10{,}000}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}.$$

If we want the population after 5 years, plug in $t=5$:

$$P(5)=\frac{10{,}000}{1+9e^{-2}} \approx \frac{10{,}000}{1+9(0.135)} \approx \frac{10{,}000}{2.215} \approx 4{,}514\text{ deer}.$$

The model shows rapid growth at first, then a slowdown as the reserve fills.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include the factor $\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$ leads to the simple exponential model, which predicts unlimited growth—unrealistic for most real‑world populations.

---

By defining the growth rate with a limit, turning the logistic idea into a differential equation, and then integrating, we obtain a powerful tool for forecasting how populations evolve over time. This step‑by‑step process mirrors many problems in calculus: start with a real‑world description, translate it into mathematics, and use limits, derivatives, and integrals to find answers.

sections.heading: 7. Reflection and Practice
sections.body:
Reflection and practice are the best ways to turn new ideas into lasting skills.  
In this part you will see how a problem can be broken into three clear stages:

1. **Limit** – find the instantaneous rate or the behaviour at a point.  
2. **Derivative** – turn that limit into a formula that works for any $x$.  
3. **Integral** – use the derivative (or its inverse) to accumulate change over an interval.

When you can recognise which stage you are in, you can choose the right tool – just like picking the right screwdriver for a screw.

> **Remember:** The three steps are a *sequence*: limit → derivative → integral.  
> If you skip a step, you may end up with an answer that looks right but is actually based on a hidden assumption.

Below is a mixed problem set. For each question, follow the guide:

* **Step 1 – Identify the limit.** Write down the limit expression that describes the situation.  
* **Step 2 – Compute the derivative.** Turn the limit into a derivative function $f'(x)$.  
* **Step 3 – Set up the integral.** Decide what quantity you need to add up (area, total change, etc.) and write the appropriate integral.  
* **Step 4 – Check.** Plug the result back into the original story to see if it makes sense.

---

### Problem 1: Speed of a car

A car’s position along a straight road is given by $s(t)=3t^{2}+2t$ meters, where $t$ is time in seconds.

1. **Limit:** Write the limit that defines the car’s instantaneous speed at time $t=4$ seconds.  
2. **Derivative:** Compute $s'(t)$, the speed function.  
3. **Integral:** Find the total distance traveled from $t=2$ s to $t=5$ s by integrating the speed.  

*Hint:* The distance is $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} s'(t)\,dt$.

---

### Problem 2: Water flowing into a tank

Water flows into a cylindrical tank at a rate that changes with time: the flow rate (in liters per minute) is $r(t)=5\sin(t)+10$, where $t$ is minutes after the tap is opened.

1. **Limit:** Express the instantaneous flow rate at $t=\pi$ minutes as a limit.  
2. **Derivative:** The flow rate itself is already a function of $t$, so $r'(t)$ would represent how the flow rate is changing. Compute $r'(t)$.  
3. **Integral:** How many liters are in the tank after 4 minutes? Use an integral of $r(t)$ from $0$ to $4$.  

*Check:* The answer should be a positive number; if you obtain a negative, you have likely reversed the limits.

---

### Problem 3: Bacterial population

A bacterial culture grows according to $P(t)=P_{0}e^{0.3t}$, where $P_{0}=200$ cells and $t$ is measured in hours.

1. **Limit:** Write the limit that gives the instantaneous growth rate at $t=3$ h.  
2. **Derivative:** Find $P'(t)$, the rate at which the number of cells changes.  
3. **Integral:** Suppose you want the total increase in cell count from $t=0$ to $t=5$ h. Set up and evaluate the integral of $P'(t)$.  

$$\int_{0}^{5} P'(t)\,dt = P(5)-P(0)$$  

*Why this works:* Integrating the derivative over an interval gives the net change of the original function.

---

### Problem 4: Temperature change

The temperature in a room (in °C) varies with time according to $T(t)=20+4\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)$, where $t$ is hours after midnight.

1. **Limit:** Write the limit that would give the instantaneous rate of temperature change at $t=6$ h.  
2. **Derivative:** Compute $T'(t)$.  
3. **Integral:** How much does the temperature increase or decrease between $t=0$ and $t=12$? Use the integral of $T'(t)$.  

*Interpretation:* A positive integral means overall warming; a negative integral means overall cooling.

---

### How to check your work

- **Units:** Make sure the units match at each step (e.g., meters per second for speed, liters for volume).  
- **Reasonableness:** Ask yourself if the number seems plausible. A car traveling at $1000\,$m/s is unrealistic, so you probably made an algebra slip.  
- **Reverse step:** After integrating, differentiate your answer. You should get back the original derivative function (up to a constant).  

> **In daily life:** Think of the three steps like a recipe. The limit is tasting a single bite to know the flavor, the derivative is writing down the full recipe, and the integral is cooking the whole meal and measuring how much you end up with.

Work through each problem slowly, writing out every limit, derivative, and integral. When you finish, compare your answers with a classmate or the answer key. The more you practice spotting the sequence, the quicker you’ll know which tool to reach for next time.

examples.title: Linear Motion – Finding Velocity
examples.given: A car travels along a straight road with position $s(t)=5t^{2}+2t$ (meters) at time $t$ seconds. Find the instantaneous velocity at $t=3\ \text{s}$.

steps.label: Differentiate Position
steps.text: Compute $v(t)=\dfrac{ds}{dt}=10t+2$ using the power rule, because velocity is the derivative of position.

examples.answer: The car’s instantaneous velocity at $3\ \text{s}$ is $32\ \text{m/s}$. ---

examples.title: Population Growth – Choosing a Model
examples.given: A town’s population $P(t)$ (in thousands) follows $P(t)=P_{0}e^{kt}$, where $t$ is years after 2020. In 2020, $P_{0}=50$. After 5 years, the population is $65$ thousand. Determine the growth rate $k$ and predict the population in 2030.

steps.label: Solve for $k$
steps.text: Divide by 50: $e^{5k}=1.3$. Take natural log: $5k=\ln 1.3$, so $k=\dfrac{\ln 1.3}{5}$.

examples.answer: The growth rate is $k\approx0.0525\ \text{yr}^{-1}$ and the predicted 2030 population is about $84.5$ thousand people. ---

examples.title: Optimizing Cost – Choosing the Right Tool
examples.given: A company can produce a widget either by manual labor (cost $C_m(x)=20x+500$ dollars for $x$ units) or by an automated machine (cost $C_a(x)=15x+1200$ dollars). Determine for which production levels $x$ the manual method is cheaper, and find the break‑even point where both costs are equal.

steps.label: Set costs equal
steps.text: Solve $20x+500=15x+1200$ to find the break‑even quantity.

steps.label: Isolate $x$
steps.text: Subtract $15x$ from both sides: $5x+500=1200$. Then subtract 500: $5x=700$.

examples.answer: The manual method is cheaper when producing fewer than $140$ widgets; the automated machine is cheaper when producing more than $140$ widgets. The break‑even point is at $x=140$ units.

practice.a:
The derivative of a polynomial is found by applying the power rule $ \frac{d}{dx}[x^n]=nx^{n-1} $.
- For $3x^2$: $ \frac{d}{dx}[3x^2]=3\cdot2x^{2-1}=6x$.
- For $5x$: $ \frac{d}{dx}[5x]=5\cdot1x^{1-1}=5$.
- For the constant $-2$: $ \frac{d}{dx}[-2]=0$.
Combine the terms: $f'(x)=6x+5$.

Factor the numerator: $x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)$.
Then $\displaystyle \frac{x^2-9}{x-3}=\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=x+3$, for $x\neq3$.
Now take the limit: $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to3}(x+3)=3+3=6$.

practice.q: A particle moves along a line with position $s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t$ (meters) for $t\ge0$. Find its velocity at $t=2$ seconds and the total distance traveled from $t=0$ to $t=3$ seconds.
practice.a:
Velocity is the derivative of position: $v(t)=s'(t)=3t^2-12t+9$.
- At $t=2$: $v(2)=3(2)^2-12(2)+9=12-24+9=-3\,$m/s.
To find total distance, locate where velocity changes sign: solve $v(t)=0$.
$3t^2-12t+9=0 \;\Rightarrow\; t^2-4t+3=0 \;\Rightarrow\; (t-1)(t-3)=0$, so $t=1$ and $t=3$.
Check intervals:
- $0\le t<1$: pick $t=0.5$, $v(0.5)=3(0.25)-12(0.5)+9=0.75-6+9=3.75>0$.
- $1<t<3$: pick $t=2$, $v(2)=-3<0$.
- $t>3$: $v$ becomes positive again.
Distance = $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}v(t)\,dt -\int_{1}^{3}v(t)\,dt$ (subtract because velocity is negative on $[1,3]$).
Compute antiderivative $S(t)=\int v(t)dt = t^3-6t^2+9t$ (which is just $s(t)$).
- $\int_{0}^{1}v(t)dt = s(1)-s(0)= (1-6+9)-(0)=4$.
- $\int_{1}^{3}v(t)dt = s(3)-s(1)= (27-54+27)-4=0-4=-4$.
Take absolute value: distance $=4-(-4)=8$ meters.

practice.q: Evaluate the definite integral $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2} (4x-5)\,dx$ and interpret its meaning as the net change of the function $F(x)=2x^2-5x$ over $[0,2]$.
practice.a:
Antiderivative of $4x-5$ is $F(x)=2x^2-5x$.
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:
$\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2} (4x-5)\,dx = F(2)-F(0)$.
Compute: $F(2)=2(2)^2-5(2)=8-10=-2$, $F(0)=0$.
Thus the integral equals $-2-0=-2$.
Interpretation: The net change of $F$ from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is $-2$; $F$ decreased by 2 units over that interval.

practice.q: The population $P(t)$ of a bacteria culture satisfies the differential equation $\displaystyle \frac{dP}{dt}=0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{5000}\right)$ with $P(0)=1000$. Find an explicit formula for $P(t)$ and determine the population after 10 hours.
practice.a:
This is a logistic differential equation: $\displaystyle \frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{M}\right)$ with $k=0.4$, $M=5000$.
Separate variables:
$\displaystyle \frac{dP}{P(1-P/5000)} = 0.4\,dt$.
Partial fractions: $\displaystyle \frac{1}{P(1-P/5000)} = \frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\,\frac{1}{5000}$.
Carrying out the decomposition gives:
$\displaystyle \frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\frac{1}{5000} = \frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\frac{1}{5000}$ (standard result).
Integrate:
$\displaystyle \int\left(\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\frac{1}{5000}\right)dP = 0.4\int dt$.
Simplify: $\displaystyle \ln|P| - \ln|5000-P| = 0.4t + C$.
Combine logs: $\displaystyle \ln\left|\frac{P}{5000-P}\right| = 0.4t + C$.
Exponentiate: $\displaystyle \frac{P}{5000-P}=Ce^{0.4t}$.
Solve for $P$: $P = 5000\frac{Ce^{0.4t}}{1+Ce^{0.4t}}$.
Use initial condition $P(0)=1000$:
$\displaystyle \frac{1000}{5000-1000}= \frac{1000}{4000}= \frac14 = C e^{0}=C$.
Thus $C= \frac14$.
Plug back:
$P(t)=5000\frac{(1/4)e^{0.4t}}{1+(1/4)e^{0.4t}} = \frac{5000 e^{0.4t}}{4+ e^{0.4t}}$.
Now compute $P(10)$:
$e^{0.4\cdot10}=e^{4}\approx 54.598$.
$P(10)=\frac{5000\cdot54.598}{4+54.598}= \frac{272990}{58.598}\approx 4662\text{ (rounded)}$.
So after 10 hours the population is about $4.66\times10^{3}$ bacteria.

Use the Taylor series for $\sin(5x)$ around $0$:
$\sin(5x)=5x-\frac{(5x)^3}{3!}+ \frac{(5x)^5}{5!}-\dots =5x-\frac{125x^3}{6}+O(x^5)$.
Subtract $5x$: $\sin(5x)-5x = -\frac{125x^3}{6}+O(x^5)$.
Divide by $x^3$: $\displaystyle \frac{\sin(5x)-5x}{x^3}= -\frac{125}{6}+O(x^2)$.
Taking the limit as $x\to0$, the $O(x^2)$ term vanishes, leaving
$\displaystyle \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(5x)-5x}{x^3}= -\frac{125}{6}$.

recap: The lesson explained limits as the value a function approaches, showed how derivatives are limits of difference quotients that give instantaneous rates of change, introduced integrals as the inverse of derivatives via the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and gave guidance on choosing between derivatives and integrals for real‑world problems.

key_terms.meaning: The value a function gets arbitrarily close to as the input approaches a certain point.
The instantaneous rate of change of a function, defined as the limit of the difference quotient.
The average rate of change (f(a+h)-f(a))/h used to define the derivative.
The accumulation of infinitely many tiny pieces, giving the total change of a function over an interval.
States that the integral of a continuous function from a to b equals an antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints, linking derivatives and integrals.
The limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero.
The maximum population size that an environment can sustain indefinitely.
A function whose derivative is the given function.

quiz.q: What does the limit lim x->a f(x)=L mean?
options: f(x) equals L for all x
f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a
L is the maximum value of f(x)
quiz.why: A limit describes the behavior of the function near a point, not necessarily at the point.

quiz.q: Which expression defines the derivative of f at x=a?
options: integral from a to a+ h of f(x) dx
quiz.why: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient as the step h approaches zero.

quiz.q: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects which two concepts?
quiz.why: It shows that integration and differentiation are inverse operations.

quiz.q: If s(t)=5t^2+2t+1, what is the instantaneous velocity at time t?
quiz.why: Differentiating s(t) gives v(t)=ds/dt=10t+2, the instantaneous velocity.

quiz.q: In a logistic growth model, what does the symbol K represent?
quiz.why: K denotes the maximum sustainable population size.

quiz.q: Which tool would you use to find the total distance traveled from t=0 to t=3 given a velocity function v(t)?
options: Average of v(t) at t=0 and t=3
quiz.why: Integrating velocity over an interval gives total distance traveled.

flashcards.back: The value a function approaches as the input gets arbitrarily close to a point.
Instantaneous rate of change; limit of the difference quotient.
(f(a+h)-f(a))/h, the average rate of change over a small interval.
Sum of infinitely many tiny pieces; gives total accumulation over an interval.
Integral of f from a to b equals antiderivative F evaluated at b minus F at a.
Limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero.
Maximum population size an environment can sustain.
A function whose derivative is the given function.
